subject: Banking
title: Mortgage-Backed Securities Fraud
description: A 60-second lesson on Mortgage-Backed Securities Fraud.

hook.text: Banks sold $2 trillion in toxic mortgage securities rated AAA. They knew the mortgages were bad. They sold them anyway.

buildup.text: Banks bundled subprime mortgages into securities and paid rating agencies to stamp them AAA.

discovery.text: Goldman Sachs created a product called Abacus, designed to fail, then bet against it.

twist.text: The fraud collapsed the global economy. 8.7 million jobs lost. $11 trillion in household wealth vanished.

climax.text: Mortgage fraud was the biggest financial scandal in history.

punchline.text: $11 trillion in losses. Banks knew. No one imprisoned. The system failed.

quiz.question: What did Goldman Sachs do with its Abacus product?
options: Sold it to clients while secretly betting it would fail

details.summary: Before the 2008 crisis, banks packaged toxic subprime mortgages into securities rated AAA, sold them to investors as safe investments, and sometimes secretly bet against the same products they were selling.
details.whyItMatters: Mortgage-backed securities fraud was the engine of the 2008 financial crisis. Banks prioritized short-term profits by selling products they knew were built on bad loans, devastating the global economy.
takeaways: Banks bundled subprime loans into complex securities rated as safe
Goldman Sachs famously bet against products it sold to clients
Taxpayers bore much of the cost through bank bailouts

faq.question: How were terrible mortgages rated as safe investments?
faq.answer: Rating agencies were paid by the banks creating the securities, creating a conflict of interest. Complex structuring tricks also made risky pools appear safer on paper than their underlying loans warranted.

faq.question: Did anyone go to jail for mortgage fraud?
faq.answer: Almost no senior bank executives were criminally prosecuted. Banks paid large fines as institutions but individuals rarely faced consequences, fueling widespread public anger about accountability in finance.
